title: A bumper crop of higher education entrants, but is university becoming less popular among the better off?
summary: It's DK's annual data spectacular on JCQ (A level and other level three outside of Scotland) results day.
full_text:
Life, as no less a philosopher than Ferris Bueller noted, comes at you pretty fast.

This is the ninth year I have analysed data on A level results and clearing for Wonkhe; it is the first time that I have a personal stake in the data.

A close member of my family (OK, my actual child, who in no way can possibly be old enough to do so…) took A levels this year, did well, and has a place on the university course of their dreams.

There is nothing unusual about that: there are 284,250 English domiciled people (61.1 per cent of all UCAS applicants from England) who have a place at their firm choice at this point on JCQ (all level 3 qualifications in England, Wales, and Northern Ireland) results day. But within these enormous datasets there are any number of personal stories – of triumph, of reckoning, or of disappointment.

We talk a lot about data and trends on Wonkhe, but behind every number is one of these stories. If that’s you, or someone you know, I’m sure there’s other things that will be more important right now than year-on-year changes and recruitment patterns.

Placed applicants and entry rates

A record 262,820 UK 18 year olds have been accepted on to a higher education course this UCAS cycle – that’s three per cent more than last year. Some 79 per cent of 18 year old applicants from England, Wales, and Northern Ireland who held an offer have been placed at their first choice of provider and course, up very slightly from last year.

In total 446,690 people are heading to a higher education provider this autumn to study. That’s another record.

Among all this record setting there is one indicator pointing another way – the JCQ results day entry rate for UK 18 year olds has fallen very slightly, from 32 per cent last year to 31.6 per cent this year. A bumper crop of 18 year olds is going through the system right now, so the numbers are higher while the proportion falls.

Here’s the state of play on results day, in comparison to previous years.

[Full screen]

You can see that, as expected, firm and insurance placements are up numerically from last year, but – unexpectedly – the proportion of firm placements has fallen for 18 year olds in England. The surprise here is that the widespread expectation was that universities would be very keen to recruit as many students as possible, and that entry requirements would be likely to flex to ensure that those who had already made a firm choice get in.

So clearing is busier this year than last (I’ll be keeping an eye on updates from tomorrow as it continues). Which will be good news for many providers.

Clearing will be a particular concern for middle and lower tariff providers. Once again, high tariff providers have been very successful in placing students, with 188,480 (a record number, which includes 117,340 UK domiciled 18 year olds) accepted on JCQ results day morning.

[Full screen]

Traditionally it is medium and lower tariff providers who do the heavy lifting in offering access to university for non-traditional students. If we look at entry rates by TUNDRA (a measure of the likelihood of people from a specific small – LSOA or equivalent – in the UK) we can see that this year’s slight overall decline in the UK 18 year old entry rate on results day (and this year’s growth in accepted applicant numbers) is reflected across all areas.

However, there has been a 0.9 percentage point decline in placement among applicants from quintile 5 (the most likely places to send 18 year olds to university) compared to just a 0.2 per cent decline from quintile 1 (the least likely) and a 0.6pp decline overall. I need hardly add that if what tends to be the best off 18 year olds were still placed in the same proportion as last year, the overall entry rate wouldn’t have fallen.

A glance back in time puts this slightly disquieting finding in context – entry rates are well above the pre-pandemic normal.

[Full screen]

It is Andy Burnham’s world, we just live in it. And as such it is worth an eye over entry rates by region. Yorkshire, the North East, and Scotland buck an overarching trend of slight decline – but London, the South East, and Northern Ireland remain more likely to send 18 year olds to university.

[Full screen]

International recruitment

Though by no means all international students arrive via UCAS (not least the growing numbers of postgraduates), there are enough of them in the system to get a sense of how recruitment is changing around the world. A large growth in the number of Chinese students placed will be good news for the Russell Group, a small but significant growth in recruitment from India is good news for larger civic providers.

Overall, UCAS-facilitated undergraduate recruitment from overseas is up about 1,000 on last year – a small growth, but not enough to mean that all of those optimistic provider predictions are correct.

[Full screen]

Level 3 results and subject choice

Though today is generally known as “A level results day” between them JCQ and DfE publish results for a whole variety of qualifications – this year sees a tidied up approach to presenting the results of vocational and technical qualifications, which means that 421 of these (covering just over 300,000 students at 307 providers) are now presented in the morning data release.

It is difficult to compare different qualifications as approaches to grading systems vary so much – and the increase in VTQ coverage means we can’t even compare year-on-year. The higher education system will be particularly interested in T level results: the fifth year of provision saw 21 T levels taught to 19,665 students (up from 11,909 last year). Of these, 92.6 per cent passed, 68.9 per cent received a merit, 18.1 per cent a distinction, and 0.4 per cent (just 74 people) the top grade of “distinction*.”

A level results are generally static year on year: a (for practical purposes) set proportion of candidates for each qualification will receive each grade, outside of the pandemic grading arrangements. Here’s a way to check that by subject area over time:

[Full screen]

You are less likely to get a high grade in some subjects rather than others, and even though this changes slightly year on year (the vagaries of mapping grades to exam performance at each awarding body) there are certain dependable observations: if you take A level law you are much less likely to be awarded a grade C or above than if you take history or economics. Here’s a visualisation to help you see how those factors played out in comparison with last year:

[Full screen]

A levels can (but do not always) inform subject choice. This year mathematics, psychology, and biology A level saw most entries – with economics the fastest growing subject(up 10 per cent on last year. And if we look at the subject areas of the higher education courses that people are entering we see a different pattern.

Two years of rapid growth in business courses has paused, while social studies (which includes economics) continues a rapid rise (up nearly 10 per cent on last year). There’s strong growth in engineering, subjects allied to medicine, psychology, and architecture – while once popular subjects like computer science and creative arts are declining.

It’s endlessly tempting to draw wider conclusions from these patterns – I’d be inclined to say this shows a growing interest in vocational subjects that link to particular career, and in high earning subjects (like economics, which tops out LEO data most years because of the ludicrously high salaries paid in the financial services sector) alongside a turning away from the more general qualifications that may offer more transferable skills. It’s what you might expect in an economy suffering a range of exogenous and endogenous pressures, and where it is so difficult for young people to enter employment.

[Full screen]

What else affects A level results?

Sitting at a desk in the school gym doing a series of very hard exams is a daunting prospect for everyone – but it isn’t just that sweaty afternoon in May that contributes to your result.

A whole host of other factors affect your ability to do your absolute best on exam day, and the first is the kind of school you attend. If your family is rich enough to pay for private school and you did A level maths, you had a 59 per cent chance of getting an A or an A* this year. If you were at your local state school, that chance was nearer 40 per cent. And if you studied at an FE college (as 4,210 people did this year), that chance was just 22.1 per cent.

[Full screen]

Likewise, the county or district you were sitting in has an impact. If you sat your maths A level aged 18 in a school in Cheltenham, you had a 70.3 per cent chance of getting an A or above. Just up the road in Tewkesbury, you are looking at 25.8 per cent. In Castle Point over in Essex, that chance was just 14.6 per cent.

[Full screen]

We often talk about A levels as if they are a perfect measure of personal achievement and aptitude for study – data like this makes it clear that where and how you live and study make a huge difference too.

full_text:
University leaders are warning of financial turmoil in British higher education after new figures suggested a collapse in international student numbers would deprive the sector of vital income and undermine its future.

The sector’s leaders called on the government to rethink the levy on international student fees imposed under Keir Starmer, as a former universities minister warned there was a risk of a university “going under” because of the financial crisis.

While UK sixth-formers enjoyed improved A-level results, and a record 194,800 English 18-year-olds were accepted by their first choice of university, vice-chancellors who spoke to the Guardian said it would not be enough to stave off further erosion in staff numbers and courses.

Figures published by the Home Office show student visa applications to the end of July fell 11% compared with the previous year. With summer visa applications coming before the start of the academic year in autumn, the gloomy figures mean many UK universities will see significant losses if the trend continues, with some fearing international enrolments dropping by 30%.

Prof Shitij Kapur, the vice-chancellor of King’s College London, said the fall in international student numbers was “in line with the pessimistic expectations” and may also reflect a drop in postgraduate applications earlier this year.

Kapur said: “The critical thing is what this cycle will entail, which does not become clear till about October. The simple rubric is that every five international students impact one university job. And these falling numbers will invariably impact the financial health and staff complement of universities.

“The silver lining in this gloomy picture is that the strength and desire to go to universities amongst our school leavers remains as strong as ever despite concerns about the loan schemes and graduate jobs, as you can see today.”

Successive governments froze domestic undergraduate fees at £9,250 between 2017 and 2025, allowing inflation to erode their value by a third. Subsequent increases will be largely wiped out by universities paying a £925 levy on each international student.

David Willetts, the Conservative former universities minister and an architect of higher tuition fees, said universities were undoubtedly “under increasing financial pressure and that’s mainly because of the freeze in fees for eight years”.

Willetts added: “There is indeed a risk of a university going under [through] financial crisis but what worries me more is just all the cutting back on the quality of the education experience of the students and I think we have an obligation to students to ensure their courses are properly funded, including by putting up fees so that the resource goes in.”

Members of the Russell Group of research-intensive universities are being affected by increased financial stress, with the University of Exeter announcing on Thursday that it was immediately scrapping geography courses at its Penryn campus in Cornwall, including for school leavers who had applied this year.

A spokesperson for Exeter said: “We recognise that this is disappointing for affected applicants and difficult for colleagues associated with these programmes.”

Libby Hackett, the chief executive of the Russell Group, said the group’s universities still attracted talented international students in an increasingly competitive global market, bringing cultural and economic benefits to their universities and to the UK more widely.

But Hackett warned: “A series of policy decisions by successive governments, including the unpopular international student levy, risks undermining this success story. This isn’t just worrying for universities – it’s not good news for the UK as a whole. Recent analysis shows that the decline in international students means the UK has lost out on a net economic benefit of nearly £3bn.

“The Burnham government recognises the critical role universities play in our national and local economies and our position on the world stage. We look forward to more consistent decision-making across government in support of economic growth, including measures that enable us to continue welcoming global talent.”

Vivienne Stern, the chief executive of the Universities UK group of vice-chancellors, said the student visa figures “should be a wake-up call” for policymakers.

“There are plenty of people in government who understand the pressure on the sector, they understand how important universities are for local economies and for domestic students, and they are watching this with concern,” Stern said. “I hope those people are knocking on the door of the [Department for Education] and the Home Office, and saying that they can do one thing tomorrow that will help universities, and that is to quietly drop the idea of taxing international student fees.

“I understand the political pressure around immigration, and the UK university sector has to be a good, responsive partner with government in making sure the system works the way it should. But if the government was seeking to reduce overseas student numbers, I think they have overcorrected. What we need is stability and a bit of help to recover our competitive position internationally.”

Jacqui Smith, the skills minister whose portfolio includes higher education, told the BBC on Thursday that the government was concerned that university courses should be good value for money, and suggested future increases in tuition fees would be linked to teaching quality.

“For most people, going to university is a very good and important investment in their future earning potential and in their life,” Smith said.

title: The Guardian view on A-level and T-level results: a boost to the nation’s confidence | Editorial
summary:
Young people should be proud of their achievements. Ministers should focus on what comes next

A strong set of A-level results should raise confidence in Britain’s future. These are difficult exams, and schools and colleges across England, Wales and Northern Ireland are rightly proud of their achievements. Top grades are up, especially in maths, which remains the most popular subject. A total of 262,820 18-year-olds have gained a place at university or college – 3% more than last year.

But the headline success masks some troubling trends. The humanities made up only a quarter of entries, while subject choices are becoming more specialised. Huge gender gaps are also striking: girls made up 79% of English A-level entries but just 19% in computing. In T-levels there has been an improvement, although their newness makes this year’s results harder to assess or compare. But the dropout rate remains higher than in the qualifications that T-levels are supposed to replace, while take-up remains low. Five years in, such ongoing issues cannot be dismissed as teething troubles.

A strong set of A-level results should raise confidence in Britain’s future. These are difficult exams, and schools and colleges across England, Wales and Northern Ireland are rightly proud of their achievements. Top grades are up, especially in maths, which remains the most popular subject. A total of 262,820 18-year-olds have gained a place at university or college – 3% more than last year.

But the headline success masks some troubling trends. The humanities made up only a quarter of entries, while subject choices are becoming more specialised. Huge gender gaps are also striking: girls made up 79% of English A-level entries but just 19% in computing. In T-levels there has been an improvement, although their newness makes this year’s results harder to assess or compare. But the dropout rate remains higher than in the qualifications that T-levels are supposed to replace, while take-up remains low. Five years in, such ongoing issues cannot be dismissed as teething troubles.

More worrying still are the geographical disparities dividing economically disadvantaged parts of the north and Midlands from the wealthy south - and especially London. Young people in the capital are almost twice as likely to apply to university as those in north-east England – the widest gap on record. Educational opportunities are diverging in parallel with economic ones.

Nor are these inequalities only spatial. There may be relief in government that private schools did not take more of the top grades; the 46.8% of their pupils receiving an A* or A was only slightly up on last year. But the fact that just 13% of college learners achieved these marks should concern everyone who wants to see all young people reach their full potential. This is arguably made more concerning by the severe financial difficulties facing some universities. The stakes in admissions have always been high, and widening inequalities between institutions could lift them higher. A 2% rise in international students accepted on to undergraduate courses should ease the sense of crisis slightly.

So far, Andy Burnham’s statements on education have pointed to devolution as his preferred method of rebalancing the system, along with a renewed focus on vocational options including new GCSEs (or equivalents). But while more firmly embedding colleges within local economies is a good idea, giving mayors responsibility for sixth forms, along with the full range of post-16 options, would be a huge shift. It must not be rushed. Rather than reorganising existing budgets, ministers should work towards a boost to spending on disadvantaged 16-19s with a scheme modelled on the pupil premium.

Looking across the qualifications landscape, A-levels are a bright spot. For too many teenagers, GCSEs are an overly restrictive or demoralising ordeal. The ability to make choices at 16 about what to study is broadly welcomed. Sixth-form and college courses can be rewarding for teachers as well as pupils – as could be seen in the videos of staff on results day. These courses and exams are not perfect; greater breadth should be a medium-term aim. But if politicians want to do right by young people, there are two things they should do right away. One is to revise the unfair terms of student loans. The other is to address the financial crisis facing the universities where many of them will be enrolling in a few weeks’ time.

From 18h ago

The gap between the proportion of A-level entries in London getting the top grades and the equivalent figure in both north-east England and the East Midlands has reached a new record size.

32.7% of entries in the capital were awarded A or A* this year, up from 32.1% in 2025 and the highest for any region in England, the exam results show.

The north-east and the East Midlands had the joint lowest rate, at 23.1%.

The gap between London and each of these two regions now stands at 9.6 percentage points, the largest since the present system of grading began in 2010, according to Press Association analysis.

In north-east England, the gap has widened from 9.2 points in 2025, though the proportion of entries getting A or A* rose slightly this year, from 22.9% to 23.1%.

By contrast, the East Midlands saw a drop in entries awarded the top grades, from 23.8% to 23.1%, the biggest fall of any region. This pushed the gap with London up from 8.3 points in 2025 to 9.6 points this year.

At a national level, 10.7% of A-level entries this year in Wales received A*, higher than the equivalent figure for England (9.6%) and Northern Ireland (8.8%).

For entries awarded A or above, Northern Ireland was ahead at 30.7%, above Wales (29.6%) and England (28.3%).

Key events

Closing summary

We are now closing the live blog.

Whatever the grades, well done to everyone who received their results today. Best of luck to those hoping to secure a university place through clearing.

For those considering university next year, we will be publishing the Guardian’s University Guide 2027 in early September with our rankings of the top universities and lots of useful advice on choosing the right course and institution for you. You can read last year’s guide here.

Here is a summary of today’s events:

Sixth-formers have basked in a summer of record-breaking exam results in academic and vocational subjects, allowing more than a quarter of a million 18-year-olds to go on to higher education. The proportion of students in England gaining the highest grade of A* in A-level subjects rose to 9.7%, up from 9.4% last year, setting a new record outside the pandemic era, when exams were scrapped.

Northern Ireland was the best-performing country, with 30.7% of grades being As and A*s, followed by 29.6% in Wales and 28.7% in England. The A-level results followed last week’s improved results in Scotland, where the proportion of students awarded Highers and Advanced Highers qualifications rose above 2019 pre-pandemic levels, and a record 18,000 Scottish school-leavers gained higher education places.

Boys have outperformed girls in terms of top grades again, after doing so for the first time in seven years last year. Overall, 28.9% of boys’ A-level entries scored an A* or A this summer, compared to 28.0% of their female classmates’ entries – a gap of 0.9 percentage points.

The gap between the proportion of A-level entries in London getting the top grades and the equivalent figure in both north-east England and the East Midlands has reached a new record size. 32.7% of entries in the capital were awarded A or A* this year, up from 32.1% in 2025 and the highest for any region in England, the exam results show.

Councils in the south of England have topped the league tables this year. In Guildford, half of all A-levels recieved an A grade or above, while Richmond in London saw 49% of grades achieve at least an A. Not all Southern areas did as well. Harlow in Essex saw just 7% of grades achieve at least an A, while Test Valley in Hampshire saw 10% (the average for England was 28%).

Results for students taking vocational and technical qualifications (VTQs) have taken a more prominent role during results day this year, after prime minister Andy Burnham declared his ambition to build parity between academic and vocational paths. More than 300,000 VTQ results across 420 qualifications were awarded, according to the Joint Council for Qualifications, with business, administration and law the most popular subject areas.

Students at private schools in England saw their top grades remain relatively flat this year – with 48.6% receiving an A* or A grade, up just 0.5 percentage points on last year. Meanwhile, students at sixth form colleges saw grades rise 0.5 points, academies saw grades rise 0.4 points, and local authority controlled comprehensives saw a 0.3 point rise. Grammar schools saw a slight fall in A and A* grades.

While the improvement in national A-level results in England is taking the headlines, social mobility experts say they are alarmed by the widening gap in performance between students in London and the south of England and their peers in other parts of the country. Nick Harrison, head of the Sutton Trust that campaigns on improving social mobility through education, said the results “reveal an increasingly stark regional divide, as London continues to pull further ahead of the rest of England”.

Shakespeare is out, while Isaac Newton is in, the figures show. This year’s results have continued the squeezing of arts and humanities subjects – which made up just over a quarter of exam entries. Ten years ago, they made up 40% of A-level exams. As we’ve written earlier, the squeeze is mainly driven by maths, other STEM subjects, and increasingly social science subjects like economics.

Exam boards pushed back on any suggestion of grade inflation after A-level students recorded record levels at A and A*. Presenting the results at a briefing by the Joint Council for Qualifications (JCQ), Richard Henry, director of qualifications and assessment at the Welsh exam board, WJEC, insisted grades could be trusted.

Results day is always governed by strict embargo, but some anxious students got their news early after the University of Surrey accidentally sent out text messages to successful applicants last night. Instead of sending the information at 8.10am Thursday morning, text messages went out to 2,400 successful applicants (about half the total) at 8.10pm last night when the nation was enjoying the eclipse.

A total of 262,820 UK 18-year-olds have gained a place at university or college – up 3% on the same point last year, according to data published by the university admissions service.

In light of Andy Burnham’s stated ambition to bridge England’s deep-rooted north-south regional divide, today’s A-level results only confirm the scale of the challenge he faces.

London continues to extend its lead with 32.7% of pupils receiving grade A or above, up from 31.9% last year. This is the largest increase of any region, and extends the gap between the capital and the north-east to 9.6 percentage points. Before Covid it was 3.9pp.

The gap in A* grades has also widened substantially, from 2 percentage points in 2019 before the pandemic – to 5.1 points in 2026.

Chris Zarraga, director of Schools North East which represents over 1,150 schools in the region, said:

There is not a north-south divide in the quality of schools or in the potential and ambition of young people. There is a structural divide in the circumstances and opportunities surrounding them.

Schools in different parts of England are not operating on a level playing field. In the north-east, schools are working within communities facing entrenched disadvantage, intense pressure on public services, growing SEND [special educational needs and disabilities] needs and very different access to opportunities and infrastructure.

Increasingly, schools are being asked to compensate for all of those things.

double quotation markThat does not mean accepting lower outcomes. These divides are not inevitable. But we will not close them simply by demanding more from schools while leaving the conditions around them unchanged.

Government needs to treat this as a system challenge. We need a long-term approach that connects education with early years, health, SEND, transport, skills and economic development, alongside high-quality academic and vocational pathways.

Results day should reflect young people’s potential and hard work, not the structural advantages or disadvantages of where they happen to grow up.

Students at private schools in England saw their top grades remain relatively flat this year – with 48.6% receiving an A* or A grade, up just 0.5 percentage points on last year.

Meanwhile students at sixth form colleges saw grades rise 0.5 points, academies saw grades rise 0.4 points, and local authority controlled comprehensives saw a 0.3 point rise. Meanwhile grammar school saw a slight fall in A and A* grades.

During the pandemic – when grades were teacher assessed – private schools saw a larger jump in top grades compared to other centres. Since then the gap between private and state funded schools has narrowed, and in recent years has remained steady.

Share

Sally Weale

Results for students taking vocational and technical qualifications (VTQs) have taken a more prominent role during results day this year, after prime minister Andy Burnham declared his ambition to build parity between academic and vocational paths.

More than 300,000 VTQ results across 420 qualifications were awarded, according to the Joint Council for Qualifications, with business, administration and law the most popular subject areas.

The number of students receiving results for T-levels – which are two-year technical education courses available in England and equivalent in size to three A-levels – jumped 65% on last year as the qualification continues to establish itself. Almost 20,000 students received results, up from 12,000 last year, with a pass rate of over 90%.

The prime minister congratulated students, saying: “It’s brilliant to see more students succeeding in T-levels, more taking maths and STEM subjects, and more young people progressing to the next stage of their education or training.

“The talent is there in every town and city in this country. Our task is to match that talent with opportunity, whether that’s through university, an apprenticeship or a technical pathway that leads to a great career. That’s how we’ll build a stronger Britain, restore hope and ensure every young person can look to the future with confidence.”

Dani Payne, head of education and social mobility at the Social Market Foundation thinktank, said today’s results showed the scale of the challenge facing the government. “T-level growth offers real encouragement for Andy Burnham’s push to put technical education on a more equal footing with academic routes.

“The number of students receiving a T-level technical qualification result has risen by around two-thirds in just one year, while outcomes remain strong, suggesting that expanding these qualifications does not have to come at the expense of standards.”

But higher education remains by far the more established and visible route for young people, she said. “More than 320,000 students received A-level results today, compared with fewer than 20,000 receiving T level results, while a record 262,820 UK 18-year-olds have already been placed at university.

“If [Burnham] wants technical education to command genuine parity of esteem, creating new pathways will only be the beginning. It will require sustained investment in further education, to ensure these new pathways lead somewhere meaningful: into good jobs, training and further study.”

Share

Richard Adams

While the improvement in national A-level results in England is taking the headlines, social mobility experts say they are alarmed by the widening gap in performance between students in London and the south of England and their peers in other parts of the country.

Nick Harrison, head of the Sutton Trust that campaigns on improving social mobility through education, said the results “reveal an increasingly stark regional divide, as London continues to pull further ahead of the rest of England”.

Harrison said:

double quotation markA young person’s chances shouldn’t depend so heavily on where they go to school, and these results underline the need for concerted action to tackle the attainment gap and regional differences across England.

Myles McGinley, managing director of the Cambridge OCR exam board, noted that even within London there were stark inequality geps between the capital’s boroughs:

double quotation markLondon’s success at a regional level is masking some severe inequalities within the capital itself. It’s a reminder that we can improve opportunities throughout the country, even in the regions that seem to be the most successful.

The proportion of top grades can more than double just by crossing the river. Almost half of every A-level result in Richmond-upon-Thames was an A or A*. In neighbouring Hounslow that figure is closer to one in five.

Share

Michael Goodier

This year’s top 10 most chosen subjects is once again the same as last year– but there has been some movement.

Once again, maths has dominated - with more than 107,000 students taking the subject in England (and that’s not including almost 20,000 further maths entries).

Economics has shot up the rankings to become the fifth most popular subject, overtaking sociology, physics and business. History was also a big winner, rising three places to become the 6th most popular subject.

Sociology fell four places – but the drop was more than made up by rises in students taking other social sciences. Politics, law and psychology – like economics – all saw significant rises in entries.

Share

Updated at 08.31 EDT

Results day is always governed by strict embargo, but some anxious students got their news early after the University of Surrey accidentally sent out text messages to successful applicants last night.

Instead of sending the information at 8.10am Thursday morning, text messages went out to 2,400 successful applicants (about half the total) at 8.10pm last night when the nation was enjoying the eclipse.

A spokesperson for the University of Surrey said:

double quotation markA scheduled results day text message was sent at the wrong time to some University of Surrey offer holders.

The information and recipients were correct, but the message was sent at 8.10pm on Wednesday rather than 8.10am on Thursday.

We are extremely sorry for this error. We self-reported to Ucas and worked closely with their team through the evening.

We immediately put in place a dedicated line for people who received the messages in error and were available to provide support through the night.

Share

Sally Weale

Among the most striking trends in A-levels this year is the surge in popularity of economics at A-level which jumped to the fifth most popular course, up from 10th position last year, with more than 47,000 entries.

Myles McGinley, managing director of the Cambridge OCR exam board, speaking at a briefing by the Joint Council for Qualifications (JCQ), said: “The students getting their A-level results today were born around 2008.

“So they’re the children of the financial crisis [and they] will have experienced the implications and impacts of that through Covid and beyond, and those forces that really shape the world.

So I think it feels natural that they should be interested in that. And of course we know that economics provides excellent career options.”

title: ‘I’m going for a few pints now’: nerves and joy as students collect their A-level results
summary:
For sixth formers in Halifax, discovering their grades means a chance to celebrate and plan for the future

There are few days that teenagers dread more than A-level results day, where students learn how the last two years of their lives will shape their futures, communicated through a few letters in an envelope.

The tension of walking into college to learn your fate is enough to keep most people awake the night before. For Hayden Bettson-Day, 18, the best solution was get it over with as early as possible.

Continue reading...
full_text:
There are few days that teenagers dread more than A-level results day, where students learn how the last two years of their lives will shape their futures, communicated through a few letters in an envelope.

The tension of walking into college to learn your fate is enough to keep most people awake the night before. For Hayden Bettson-Day, 18, the best solution was get it over with as early as possible.

“I was refreshing the Ucas page at 8 o’clock in the morning, waiting for it to go on,” Hayden said. “So, it was a definite bit of tension. My mum kept asking: ‘What is it? What did you get?”

What Hayden got was an A* in maths coupled with two As in chemistry and biology, which is enough to be accepted into Newcastle University to study medicine.

The 18-year-old is one of 450 students at Trinity sixth form academy, located in the town’s centre and part of the Trinity multi-academy trust, which has colleges throughout Yorkshire.

Aidan Chiu and Fran Whitehead, two of Hayden’s classmates, spoke about their own relief at their results, having both received A*s in chemistry.

“My mum’s on the phone to Bristol University,” said Aidan, who plans to study maths. “I have the grades I need, but she’s still calling them to make sure I got in. I can’t believe it.”

Fran, who will now study geology at the University of Exeter, said that the last two years had been difficult, but praised the college for helping her settle and supporting her as she readjusted to a new environment during such a pivotal time in her life.

“I came to this school knowing nobody, but all the teachers and students were really nice and I found my place,” said Fran. “You’ve got lots of support to achieve your potential.”

Not every student was as optimistic about their results, with some planning to go through clearing or committing themselves to return to sixth form to achieve the grades they desired.

In Natalia Ntabola’s case, the plan was more straightforward: “If I didn’t get into university, I was just going to move out of the country and live somewhere off the grid, to be honest.”

Luckily for Natalia, she and lifelong best friend Sandra Konarska, both 18, got the grades that the pair needed in order to attend the University of Manchester together.

Sandra, who felt that she “may not have revised as much as she should have” despite being awarded a perfect three A*s, lauded the college for the amount of effort and encouragement that they have given her.

“I think the teachers are very rigorous, there’s a lot of homework to do, a lot of meetings and talks if it’s not done,” said Sandra. “They’re very adamant on it being complete, but it works.”

Michael Fitzsimons, the principal of Trinity sixth form academy, attributes the college’s success to the ethics of hard work and commitment, but also stresses the sixth form’s commitment to bringing in students from all backgrounds and abilities.

“We don’t ever want people to feel sorry for our kids,” said Fitzsimons. “Where we are, there is around double the level of disadvantage to the rest of the country, but that doesn’t change the expectations. We still hold them to high expectations, but that’s delivered with a lot of love.”

To get their students ready for the realities of life beyond Halifax, the college funds a “scholars programme” scheme to give high achieving students free access to tutors from some of the country’s top universities, not to coach them through exams, but to help raise their confidence and interviewing skills, increasing their belief that they will not be out of place around any future peers who may have come from a more affluent background.

The college has also helped subsidise trips abroad, including trips to New York City and Brussels. Joe Kirwan, who went on both trips and achieved three As, plans to attend the University of Nottingham. He says that teachers at the college went above and beyond to help him, even “recommending podcasts and giving me books, trying to make me believe I can do what they think I can do”.

Now, with the tension of the morning relieved, the students are celebrating in a variety of ways, ranging from meals with their families, playing board games with their friends and having a nap. The majority, as expected, have set off for the pubs in Halifax town centre, including Hayden.

“I’m going for a few pints now,” he said. “I’m going to Newcastle for the next few years and I’ve heard about the nightlife, so I need to start practising.”

title: Behind England’s bumper A-level results lie record levels of regional disparities
summary:
Need for Burnham to tackle regional inequality could not be clearer as London becomes ‘educational outlier’

Andy Burnham has put regional inequality at the top of his agenda as prime minister, and nowhere is the need for doing so clearer than in education.

As England’s A-level results were published on Thursday morning, students across the country were pictured celebrating a bumper crop of results, with record rates of As and A*s.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Andy Burnham has put regional inequality at the top of his agenda as prime minister, and nowhere is the need for doing so clearer than in education.

As England’s A-level results were published on Thursday morning, students across the country were pictured celebrating a bumper crop of results, with record rates of As and A*s.

Drill down into the detail, however, and the regional disparities are shocking, with the gap between London and the lowest performing areas of the country also at record levels.

Nearly a third of A-level candidates in the capital (32.7%) gained A*s and As, up six percentage points on last year.

In the East Midlands, however, less than a quarter (23.1%) secured top grades, down from 23.8% in 2025, putting it level with the north-east, which increased its share of top grades marginally from 22.9% last year.

The results reveal the gap in A and A* grades between London and the north-east has grown to an alarming 9.6 percentage points, the largest since the pandemic and significantly higher than the 2019 pre-pandemic disparity of 3.9 points.

The gap in A* grades is up from two percentage points in 2019 to 5.1 points in 2026. Experts are hoping the prime minister’s devolution plans to give regional areas the independence to adapt their approach to local conditions will help learners outside London.

Lee Elliot Major, a professor of social mobility at Exeter University, said: “Our capital has become an educational outlier while too many young people in the north-east, East Midlands and other parts of the country are growing up in very different worlds of opportunity.

“England is no longer defined by a simple north-south divide. It is increasingly a story of London pulling away from much of the country. Talent is spread evenly across the country; opportunity is not.”

The reasons for London’s runaway success are many. Tony Blair’s London Challenge started the process of transformation in the capital’s schools in 2003. Since then higher pay and cultural attractiveness have incentivised more teachers to join the capital’s schools, while ambitious migrant families have helped raise standards.

The Department for Education says its Rise teams (regional improvement for standards and excellence) are putting “a laser focus” on areas and schools where performance is weakest.

A proposal in the schools white paper to use household income to vary funding rates according to the level of disadvantage so that children with more entrenched disadvantage attract more funding has also been welcomed.

But the scale and persistence of the disparities laid bare in Thursday’s results clearly require significant intervention.

Chris Zarraga, the director of Schools North East, which represents 1,150 schools in the region, said schools in different parts of England were not operating on a level playing field.

“In the north-east, schools are working within communities facing entrenched disadvantage, intense pressure on public services, growing Send [special educational needs and disabilities] needs and very different access to opportunities and infrastructure.

“Increasingly, schools are being asked to compensate for all of those things. That does not mean accepting lower outcomes. These divides are not inevitable. But we will not close them simply by demanding more from schools while leaving the conditions around them unchanged. Government needs to treat this as a system challenge.”

He called for a long-term approach encompassing education, early years, health, Send, transport, skills and economic development, alongside high-quality academic and vocational pathways.

Elliot Major said an “ambitious, region-first approach” was needed. “Too many rural, coastal and post-industrial communities have been left with fewer educational and economic opportunities.

“The warning lights are flashing: persistent attainment gaps by background and place, historically high levels of school absence, and growing divides outside the school gates.

Daniel Kebede, the general secretary of the National Education Union, said more funding was needed. “Schools do everything they can to respond to poverty but the pressures and strains on schools in areas of disadvantage must be addressed by Andy Burnham’s government, including all our schools and colleges to be properly funded.”

Zarraga said: “Results day should reflect young people’s potential and hard work, not the structural advantages or disadvantages of where they happen to grow up.”

title: Five key takeaways from results day 2026
summary: Top grades and students going to university are on the up, but technical subjects are also becoming more popular.
full_text:
Results for A-levels, T-levels, BTecs and other vocational qualifications are out.

And this year, they've come at a time when all eyes are on what teenagers decide to do next.

Universities are keen to get them through the door. As they grapple with their finances, they know that every filled seat in a lecture hall comes with tuition fee funding.

The new prime minister, meanwhile, wants to carve out clear routes into technical jobs that can rival the well-established path of A-levels and a university degree.

For teenagers, considerations about the immediate and long-term cost of university, as well as the availability of other options, are all in the mix.

Here are the standout things you need to know.

About 40% of 18-year-olds in England receive A-levels every summer, and this year top A-level results across the whole of England, Wales and Northern Ireland have risen for a third year running.

Overall, 28.5% of grades were marked at A* or A, up from 28.3% last year.

The results are still much lower than they were in 2020 and 2021, when exams were cancelled and results were based on teachers' assessments.

After that, there was a concerted effort to bring them back down. Grading in England returned to pre-pandemic levels in 2023 – prompting a big fall in top grades – while Wales and Northern Ireland followed suit in 2024.

The proportion of top grades across the three nations combined has been slightly creeping up since that drop in 2023.

The proportion of A-levels marked at A* and A was:

28.3% in England, up from 28.2% in 2025

29.6% in Wales, up from 29.5%

30.7% in Northern Ireland, up from 30.3%

You can see how results were in your local area using the look-up tool below.

A record number of 18-year-olds in the UK have been accepted into university, according to the Universities and Colleges Admissions Service (Ucas) - with more than ever getting into their first choice.

The steepest growth has been in acceptances to what Ucas calls "higher tariff" universities. These are the most selective institutions, like those in the Russell Group.

They have taken on 5.5% more UK 18-year-olds than last year, and many are still advertising courses in Clearing.

Nick Hillman, chief executive of the Higher Education Policy Institute, said a fall in the number of postgraduate international students had freed up resources for universities to teach more UK undergraduates, and the Russell Group stressed its members would "only admit students who show evidence of being able to succeed".

Still, four in 10 universities in England are expected to report a financial deficit in 2025-26, squeezed by a long-term freeze in domestic tuition fees and a fall in international student numbers. Taking on more UK students may offer some financial stability for those selective universities, but other institutions will be hoping to recruit more students through Clearing.

Jo Saxton, chief executive of Ucas, told the BBC the sheer amount of courses listed in Clearing meant teenagers could "absolutely still go to university in the autumn if that's what they would like to do".

That might be welcome news for some. While the raw number of 18-year-olds getting into their first choice has risen, there are more of them in the population than in previous years - and the actual percentage of 18-year-old offer-holders in England, Wales and Northern Ireland getting into their first choice has fallen from 82% to 79%.

Universities aren't the only ones worried about their finances. Teenagers, too, are concerned about the cost of going to university, and Saxton said many were using Clearing to find courses closer to home.

But ultimately, the percentage of UK 18-year-olds applying to university has remained stable, and worries about the long-term costs - with rising tuition fees and widespread criticism of the student loans system - do not appear to have put teenagers off.

This is the fifth year of T-level results in England, and the number of students getting grades has rocketed as their rollout continues.

More than 19,600 students received grades in 21 subjects this year, up from 11,900 students across 18 subjects last year.

This will be welcome news for the new prime minister, who says he wants pupils in England to be able to study technical subjects in addition to core academic learning from Year 10.

The pass rate increased slightly from 91.4%, according to last year's provisional results, to 92.6%. And the percentage of students achieving a merit or above grew from 65.3% to 68.9%.

The dropout rate remains high, though – and some students take longer than the standard two-years to complete the course. Around 77% of students who started their T-level in 2024, and were therefore expected to complete it this year, have received results.

T-levels are among the 300,000 grades for vocational and technical qualifications released today.

That's still much smaller than the number of A-level grades given out (more than 800,000 among 18-year-olds alone).

But there are indications that interest in technical education is on the rise. According to Ucas, engineering and technology subjects saw the biggest growth in university acceptances, up 16% from last year.

More A* and A grades went to girls than boys this year – 137,000 compared to 120,900.

But more girls sit A-levels in the first place, and looking at the percentage of boys and girls getting these top grades suggests that boys are actually doing better.

This year, 28.9% of all grades given to boys were A*s and As, compared to 28% of grades given to girls.

It used to be the other round, and last year was the first year boys overtook girls in this respect since 2018. Now, that gap has widened.

Girls are still outperforming boys when you look at a broader range of grades, though.

For example, 79.8% grades given to girls were marked A* to C, compared to 76.8% of boys' grades.

title: College Wasn’t Built for Student Parents
summary:
College Wasn’t Built for Student Parents
Joshua.Bay Thu, 08/13/2026 - 03:00 AM

In this week’s Voices of Student Success episode, Generation Hope’s Nicole Lynn Lewis explores how colleges can better support student parents and caregivers.

Byline(s)
Joshua Bay
full_text:
One in five undergraduate students is a parent or caregiver, balancing coursework and college life with the responsibility of caring for someone else. Yet higher education systems and policies often weren’t designed with those students in mind.

From finding affordable childcare and stable housing to navigating time poverty, financial insecurity and questions of belonging, student parents face barriers that can shape their ability to persist and ultimately earn a degree.

Nicole Lynn Lewis, founder and chief executive officer of Generation Hope, joined Inside Higher Ed student success reporter Joshua Bay on Voices of Student Success to discuss what colleges still misunderstand about student parents and the challenges they navigate both in and outside the classroom.

Here are five takeaways on what institutions can do to better support student parents and caregivers.

Follow us on Apple Podcasts and Spotify

Student parents aren’t a niche population.

Lewis said 20 percent of undergraduates are student parents or caregiving students, underscoring that they are not a niche population in higher education, even if they are often overlooked in conversations about today’s college students.

“That’s part of the work that we have to do in higher education is to help anyone sitting around a kitchen table understand that the student-parent population is a significant population,” Lewis said. “The more awareness we bring to this, the more understanding that people have about the student-parent experience.”

She noted that these students are often juggling coursework with bedtime routines and staying up late to finish assignments as they navigate childcare, among other responsibilities. But understanding the size and experiences of the student-parent population also has implications beyond higher education, Lewis said.

“It helps people to think about all of the ancillary kinds of connected issues,” Lewis said. “Helping student parents get through college is a part of the solution to dismantling poverty. It’s part of the solution to advancing economic mobility.”

Childcare is only one of the barriers student parents face.

Lewis said student parents need childcare like they need oxygen, noting that “instead of treating it as a nice-to-have, we really need to be looking at childcare as an absolute critical component to our economic engine.”

However, she said, childcare is only one piece of a much larger puzzle.

“We really need to be looking at transportation, for example,” Lewis said. “Do students have reliable public transportation options to get to campus? Are there emergency grants that can help them when their car breaks down and they need to get to campus?”

In addition, Lewis noted that housing insecurity is another major barrier for student parents, drawing on her own experience attending college with a 3-month-old daughter.

“I started at William and Mary when my daughter was a little under 3 months old, and I quickly came into a housing crisis,” Lewis said. “I was able to find a loophole in their housing that allowed me, as an undergraduate, to take advantage of their family housing that was really intended for graduate students and professors with families.”

“That was just luck,” she added. “But for most students who are going to a four-year school and have a baby or have dependents, they don’t have family housing options.”

Lewis also pointed to “time poverty”—the reality that many student parents have little discretionary time in their day—as another barrier that institutions often overlook.

“When you’re a parenting student, you’re juggling work, the needs of your children, doctor’s appointments, school meetings, coursework, all of those things,” Lewis said. “It’s incredibly important that we’re thinking about if we have, for example, a process or a policy that requires a student to make three trips to one of our administrative offices to be able to qualify for a scholarship or to be able to apply for an opportunity … how is that creating exclusions for our parenting students?”

Student parents need to know they belong on campus.

Lewis said belonging is something that cuts across all student demographics but can be particularly complicated for student parents and caregivers, who may enter college already expecting that they won’t be in traditional campus structures.

“For student parents, you go into the higher ed experience expecting to not be included, expecting to not belong, and I think simple things can go such a long way,” Lewis said.

She noted that including student parents and caregivers in campus brochures, websites and newsletters to donors are small ways institutions can signal that these students are part of the campus community.

“It’s the big investments, the childcare center, the big kind of multimillion-dollar investments that are necessary,” Lewis said. “But also, it can be the small things like having toys in your waiting area, having those photos of caregiving students in your collateral, profiling a student parent in your newsletter to donors.”

“How are we communicating that belonging at every level and making sure it’s permeating an institution and everyone is on the same page on how we are really being intentional about saying, ‘You do belong here’?” she added.

Supporting student parents requires more than adding services.

Lewis noted that, thankfully, more institutions are offering family resource centers, childcare programs and emergency grants specifically for student parents. But what separates an institution that truly serves student parents from one that simply adds services is whether that support is embedded across the institution.

“It’s not just one office that’s doing certain things. We want to see that change and that transformation happening across every department,” Lewis said.

That means involving people across the institution, she said—even those in departments that may not traditionally be viewed as part of student-parent support, such as facilities.

“Oftentimes people say, ‘Well, why do you have the facilities people around the table for this work?’ Well, we are helping to figure out how we can get more high chairs into the dining spaces. We're helping to figure out how to make sure more restrooms for all genders have diaper-changing stations,” Lewis said.

“What we want to see is that an institution has ensured that there are supports, there are services, there are accommodations, there are ways that that student feels that they belong, no matter whether they’re getting a parking pass or going to get their financial aid package,” she added.

Student parents bring strengths colleges too often overlook.

Lewis said it’s important for institutions to recognize the strengths student parents and caregivers bring to campus, noting that they often demonstrate strong academic performance and a deep determination to succeed.

“One of the things that I ask college leaders is ‘When you think about student parents, do you think of them as a liability or as an asset?’” Lewis said. “They are incredibly driven. They're leaders at home. They can be leaders in our campus communities, so this is an opportunity to engage untapped leaders.”

She pointed to her own experience as a student parent as an example of the motivation many bring to their education.

“In college there wasn’t a plan B for me. I had to get that college degree to provide for my daughter, so every day, that was what my focus was,” Lewis said. “As I look at the scholars in our program and the many student parents I’ve met across the country, that same drive and incredible motivation is there.”

title: Survey Shows Students Trust College Leaders More Than Politicians
summary:
Survey Shows Students Trust College Leaders More Than Politicians
Olivia.sanchez Thu, 08/13/2026 - 03:00 AM

Students from all political parties reported higher approval of campus-led policies, compared to state and federal policies, according to data from Gallup and Lumina Foundation.

Byline(s)
Olivia Sanchez
full_text:
College students are roughly split on whether they think institutional leaders have their best interests at heart, according to new survey data from Gallup and the Lumina Foundation published Thursday. Fifty-five percent of students said they felt administrators act in students’ best interest most or all of the time, while 45 percent said they thought leaders made decisions in their best interest sometimes, rarely or never.

The survey, which examined students’ perceptions of who influences their college experience, found that state and federal officials also played a role. With policy shifts affecting research funding, curriculum, diversity initiatives and more, 58 percent of undergraduate students reported that federal or state policies contributed to at least a moderate change on campus. And although students were divided on trust in campus leadership and the effects of federal and state policies, survey data showed that students from all political parties reported higher approval of campus-led policies compared to state and federal policies. While 79 percent of respondents approved of decisions made by their institution’s leaders, only 56 percent said they approved of such policies made by state leaders and 45 percent approved of federal policy decisions affecting their campus.

Trust in campus leadership varied depending on the type of institution students attended. Community college students reported slightly higher levels of trust in their institutional leaders compared to their peers at four-year institutions, the data showed. Students enrolled at the most selective colleges reported lower levels of trust than their peers at all other institutions. When broken down by political affiliation, 62 percent of Republican-identified students said their campus leaders act in students’ best interest all or most of the time, compared to 55 percent of students who identified as Democrats.

Over all, the students surveyed expressed more confidence in higher education than the broader American public, whose trust in the sector has fallen precipitously over the last decade. The decaying trust is due in large part to the high cost of college, perceived political agendas in the classroom and concerns about adequate workforce preparation, according to a Gallup report released in 2025. That survey found that 42 percent of American adults reported a great deal of trust in higher ed in 2025, down from 57 percent in 2015. The results showed that trust was the lowest in 2024, when 36 percent reported a great deal of trust, 32 percent reported some trust and 32 percent reported little or no trust in higher education.

Although the Gallup and Lumina survey suggests mixed trust in institutional leaders, past Inside Higher Ed Student Voice surveys show that students have greater trust in faculty (whom they trust the most) and advisers than in administrators and executive-level leaders (whom they trust the least).

title: Nearly a quarter of the nation’s children are chronically absent from school in ‘ominous’ trend: researchers
summary: Absenteeism is down since peaking during pandemic, but districts across the country are still struggling
full_text:
Nearly a quarter of U.S. students were chronically absent from school last year in what researchers called an “ominous” trend for the education system.

In 2025, 22.6 percent of students missed 10 percent or more of the school year, the American Enterprise Institute found.

That’s down from a high of 28.3 percent in 2022, during the peak of the Covid pandemic, but chronic absenteeism remains above pre-pandemic levels — and gains in stopping it appear to be slowing with each passing year.

AEI called the trend “an ominous slowdown that should be met with urgent action, not ignominious acceptance.”

Chronic absenteeism can cause a host of problems.

“Missing school means missing valuable instructional time and poses serious implications for students' overall academic success and wellbeing,” according to the U.S. Department of Education. “Research suggests that children who are chronically absent for multiple years between preschool and second grade are much less likely to read at grade level by the third grade.”

Alaska, Washington, D.C., Oregon and New Mexico had the highest absenteeism rates, AEI found, while New Jersey, Virginia and Alabama had the lowest.

The phenomenon tends to be clustered in historically disadvantaged districts, the think tank notes.

In Illinois, for example, the general chronic absenteeism rate was about 25 percent last year, while 31 percent of low-income students were chronically absent and nearly 40 percent of Black students were.

Educators across the country have been trying different strategies to get students back to class.

In Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, where 32 percent of students were chronically absent last year, an organization called A+ Schools has been reaching out directly to families, offering supplies and transportation as school gets back underway.

"Today is about bridging that gap, going and knocking on doors, letting folks know about what's available at the school to help them out," James Fogarty with A+ Schools told CBS Pittsburgh.

A related phenomenon known as school avoidance, where students refuse to attend class or struggle to remain in school for the full day, can also contribute to absences. School avoidance is pronounced among disabled students.

New York City recently settled a lawsuit accusing its public school system of failing to spot early warning signs of avoidance and thus denying disabled students a full education.

The school system now has a plan to put liaisons in every school building to monitor for challenges that keep students out of school, such as mental health struggles.

title: CATE 2026: From campus to community: a student-led health clinic
summary: The post CATE 2026: From campus to community: a student-led health clinic appeared first on Advance HE UK.
full_text:
Professor Hamde Nazar, Royal College of Surgeons Ireland and Newcastle University, on how the CATE 2026 winner, Young@Heart clinic, turns pharmacy students into community health champions.

8,000 health checks.

700 students.

4 published papers, and counting.

Since 2019, a small stall in Newcastle’s Grainger Market has quietly become one of the busiest classrooms at our university, and one of the city’s most trusted health services.

The Young@Heart (Y@H) clinic offers free cardiovascular screening, checking blood pressure, cholesterol, blood glucose and Body Mass Index, alongside advice on healthier lifestyle choices and signposting to other services, such as smoking cessation support. What makes it different is who runs it: undergraduate pharmacy students, supervised by academic staff, deliver the entire service themselves.

We set up Y@H to solve two problems at once. Clinical placements for pharmacy students were becoming harder to find, at the same time as we saw real unmet health need in our local community. Rather than treat these as separate issues, we built a clinic that addresses both, giving students authentic clinical experience while taking preventative health care directly to the people who need it most.

Students in the driving seat

What sets Y@H apart is that students run it, not just staff it. They manage the daily rota, triage patients, interpret results, make clinical decisions, and have the difficult conversations about lifestyle change, all under supervision, but with real ownership. Along the way they build skills that go well beyond the pharmacy curriculum: time management, delegation, teamwork and confidence under pressure.

One student summed up the shift in themselves plainly: “my technique and my consultation skills have definitely got a lot better… I’m so confident with doing what I’m doing.” Another spoke about the sense of purpose the clinic gives them: “providing this service to people feels good, that we can give back to the public.”

A ripple effect beyond pharmacy

What started as a pharmacy initiative has grown well beyond it. Students from sports and exercise science now take part, as do international students from our partner institution, Loyola. The model has also travelled further afield: schools of pharmacy at De Montfort and Liverpool John Moores, and medical schools at Warwick and the Royal College of Surgeons in Ireland, have adopted versions of the Y@H approach. Members of the team were recently invited to share the model with educators across NHS Scotland.

None of this happened by accident. From the outset, the clinic has been built on genuine co-creation: academic, technical and research colleagues working alongside students to shape everything from clinic design to evaluation. When we opened a dedicated clinic space in Grainger Market in 2024, we deliberately sought input from local authority partners, third-sector organisations and students themselves, to make sure the space worked for the public as well as for learning.

Making a difference where it matters most

The clinic’s community impact is where the numbers really land. In one evaluation of over 1,150 people, a third came from the most deprived areas of the North East, a group with high rates of overweight and obesity (62%), raised cholesterol (36%) and high blood pressure (44%). Encouragingly, people’s intentions to change their health behaviour increased significantly after visiting the clinic.

That reach continues to grow through partnerships with HealthWorks, the Action Foundation, St Vincent’s Centre and Newcastle GP Partners, as well as a community health bus that takes the service to people who might otherwise face barriers to care. Local press coverage of the clinic and the health bus reflects just how much this work matters to the city, not just the university.

Evidence at the core

We’ve made a point of evaluating everything we do, and it shows: four published papers (with three more under review), presentations at international conferences, and award nominations including the THE Awards and the Academic Health Science Network’s Bright Ideas in Health Awards. That evidence base means the model isn’t just a nice story, it’s a replicable blueprint that other institutions can adapt with confidence.

Six years on, Y@H has shown that clinical education and community benefit don’t have to be traded off against each other. Give students real responsibility, build genuine partnerships, and measure what happens, and you can improve outcomes for students and the public at the same time.

Could a similar model work in your discipline, or your institution?

Hamde Nazar is Professor of Pharmacy and Deputy Head of School at Royal College of Surgeons and leads the Young@Heart student-led clinic team, researching student-led service learning and clinical pharmacy education.

Un terreno molto più complesso della semplice installazione di pannelli, che si misura oggi il futuro delle Comunità Energetiche Rinnovabili (CER). Per sostenerle il Consiglio di amministrazione di Fondazione Cariverona ha approvato 323.200 euro a favore di 13 CER presenti nelle province di Verona, Vicenza, Belluno e Ancona. Non si tratta di nuove iniziative sulla carta, ma di un sostegno a realtà già costituite, chiamate ora a rafforzare organizzazione, gestione e capacità di produrre benefici per i territori.

Il nuovo intervento rappresenta una nuova tappa del programma avviato nel 2023. Dopo la progettazione, la selezione e l’accompagnamento delle reti territoriali, il percorso ha sostenuto la costituzione delle CER e, nel 2025, il loro consolidamento organizzativo, energetico e sociale. Le risorse approvate per il 2026 finanziano i piani operativi di potenziamento e sviluppo presentati dalle comunità, con l’obiettivo di accrescerne l’autonomia, rafforzarne la capacità gestionale e aumentarne le ricadute sui territori.

«Le innovazioni capaci di incidere sulla vita delle persone non nascono già perfette: vanno sperimentate, misurate e accompagnate», afferma Bruno Giordano, presidente di Fondazione Cariverona. «Per questo non ci siamo fermati alla costituzione delle comunità energetiche né all’erogazione di un primo contributo. Abbiamo scelto di restare al loro fianco nel passaggio più delicato, quello in cui un’idea deve diventare organizzazione, competenza e servizio. Il ruolo di una fondazione è anche questo: assumersi il rischio dell’innovazione, aiutare i territori a imparare e trasformare le sperimentazioni più promettenti in capacità che rimangono».

I progetti presentati riflettono condizioni territoriali, organizzative e tecniche differenti, ma condividono alcuni fabbisogni centrali: gestire soci, impianti e flussi energetici, completare le procedure con il GSE, rafforzare le competenze interne e ampliare la partecipazione di produttori e consumatori. Le risorse saranno quindi utilizzate per la gestione tecnica e amministrativa, la formazione, gli strumenti digitali, l’aggiornamento dei piani economici e il coinvolgimento delle comunità locali.
